lede: Water crosses the membrane of every cell on its own, from a dilute solution into a more concentrated one. That one movement makes a plant firm or limp, and it is the whole of Prescribed Practical B5.
can: Explain osmosis and say which way water moves in any set-up.
Describe turgid and plasmolysed cells, and why a plant cell does not burst.
Work out and read percentage changes from potato cylinders and Visking bags.

md: **Osmosis** is the diffusion of **water** molecules out of a **dilute** solution and into a **more concentrated** one, through a **selectively permeable membrane**. The membrane lets small molecules such as water through and holds large ones, such as sugar, back.

title: Why water goes that way
md: A dilute solution holds **more water** in each cubic centimetre, so more water molecules strike the membrane from that side each second. More cross one way than the other: the **net** movement is into the concentrated solution.

stem: A selectively permeable membrane separates 5 per cent sugar solution from 20 per cent sugar solution. Say which way water moves, and whether the sugar moves. [2]

steps.working: Water moves from the 5 per cent side into the 20 per cent side.
steps.decision: The 5 per cent solution is the dilute one: more water per cubic centimetre, so more water crosses from it.

steps.working: The sugar does not cross.
steps.decision: Its molecules are too large for the membrane. Sugar spreading out would be diffusion, but it would not be osmosis, which is water only.

title: Membrane Transport

task: Put a different number of particles on each side of the membrane and watch which way the net movement goes. Then say in one sentence why a carrot cylinder in pure water gains mass, using the words dilute, concentrated and selectively permeable.

prompt: A selectively permeable membrane separates pure water from a 10 per cent salt solution. Which way does water move overall?
options: from the pure water into the salt solution
from the salt solution into the pure water
there is no overall movement
answer: from the pure water into the salt solution
explain: Pure water is the most dilute solution there is, so water moves from it into the salt solution, the more concentrated one. The See it moved water from 5 per cent into 20 per cent the same way.

optionNotes.option: from the salt solution into the pure water
optionNotes.why: It tempts because salt is the thing that seems to spread, but osmosis is water moving into the more concentrated solution.

optionNotes.option: there is no overall movement
optionNotes.why: No overall movement needs the two sides at the same concentration; pure water and salt solution are not.

twin.prompt: A selectively permeable membrane separates 2 per cent sucrose solution from 8 per cent sucrose solution. Which way does water move overall?
options: from the 2 per cent into the 8 per cent solution
from the 8 per cent into the 2 per cent solution
there is no overall movement
twin.answer: from the 2 per cent into the 8 per cent solution
twin.explain: The 2 per cent solution is the more dilute, so water moves out of it and into the 8 per cent solution.

optionNotes.option: from the 8 per cent into the 2 per cent solution
optionNotes.why: That is the reverse: water moves into the stronger solution, not out of it.

optionNotes.option: there is no overall movement
optionNotes.why: The two concentrations differ, so there is a net movement of water.

caption: Compare the two liquids, inside and outside, before you say anything about the water.

md: A plant cell's sap is itself a solution. So always name **both** liquids, the cell sap and the solution outside, and decide which is the more concentrated.

Outside **weaker**: water moves in and the tissue gains mass. Outside **stronger**: water moves out and it loses mass. Outside **equal**: water still crosses both ways, but there is **no net movement**, so the mass does not change.

stem: Three carrot cylinders are left in pure water, in a solution as concentrated as their cell sap, and in a stronger solution. Describe what happens to each, and why. [3]

steps.working: Pure water: water moves in and the cylinder gains mass.
steps.decision: The cell sap is the more concentrated of the two liquids.

steps.working: Equal solution: no net movement, so no change in mass.
steps.decision: Water crosses both ways at the same rate, so nothing changes overall.

steps.working: Stronger solution: water moves out and the cylinder loses mass.
steps.decision: Now the outside is the more concentrated liquid.

prompt: A potato cylinder neither gains nor loses mass in a 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution. What does that tell you?
options: its cell sap is about as concentrated as 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
osmosis has stopped completely in its cells
its membranes have stopped letting water through
answer: its cell sap is about as concentrated as 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
explain: No change in mass means no net movement of water, and that happens when the cell sap and the solution are equally concentrated. Water still crosses both ways, as in the equal case of the See it.

optionNotes.option: osmosis has stopped completely in its cells
optionNotes.why: Water still crosses the membrane both ways; it is only the net movement that is zero.

optionNotes.option: its membranes have stopped letting water through
optionNotes.why: The membranes still let water through; equal concentrations make the movement balance.

twin.prompt: A potato cylinder loses mass in a 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution. What does that tell you about its cell sap?
options: it is more dilute than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
it is more concentrated than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
it is as concentrated as 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
twin.answer: it is more dilute than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
twin.explain: Water left the cells, so it moved towards the solution: the solution outside was the more concentrated, and the cell sap the more dilute.

optionNotes.option: it is more concentrated than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
optionNotes.why: If the sap were the stronger, water would have moved in and the cylinder gained mass.

optionNotes.option: it is as concentrated as 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
optionNotes.why: Equal concentrations give no change in mass; this cylinder lost mass.

md: A cell that takes in water is **turgid**: its vacuole is full and presses the cytoplasm and membrane against the cell wall. Many turgid cells pressing on their neighbours make a plant firm.

A cell that loses a lot of water is **plasmolysed**: the vacuole and cytoplasm get **smaller** and the **membrane pulls away from the cell wall**. The wall, rigid cellulose, does not move. In between, the cell is limp (flaccid), but CCEA's papers name only turgid and plasmolysed.

alt: Light micrograph of red onion epidermis cells after being mounted in a concentrated solution: each cell keeps a straight-sided rigid wall, while the red-purple contents have shrunk into a rounded blob that has separated from the wall, leaving a clear gap.
credit: Trương Minh Khải, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
caption: Red onion cells in a strong solution. The straight lines are the walls; the coloured blobs are the contents, pulled in.
prompt: The examiner shows you this and asks what has happened to the cell membrane. What is the one sentence that earns the mark — and why is 'the cell wall has pulled away' not it?

stem: A drawing shows a cell from a celery stalk left in a strong salt solution. Give two features of the drawing that show it has lost water. [2]

steps.working: The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall.
steps.decision: Name the moving part first: the membrane, never the wall.

steps.working: The vacuole is small.
steps.decision: A second, separate feature earns the second mark; the cytoplasm being smaller would do as well.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Osmosis"
why: A second look at cells gaining and losing water, beside the worked features.

prompt: In the photograph of red onion cells in a strong solution, which structure has moved?
options: the cell membrane, pulling away from the wall
the cell wall, pulling away from the membrane
both, pulling away from each other
answer: the cell membrane, pulling away from the wall
explain: The walls keep their straight sides because rigid cellulose does not move; the shrinking contents pull the membrane inwards, away from the wall. The See it's first feature named the membrane in the same way.

optionNotes.option: the cell wall, pulling away from the membrane
optionNotes.why: The walls keep their shape in the photograph; it is the contents and their membrane that shrink.

optionNotes.option: both, pulling away from each other
optionNotes.why: Only the contents shrink; the rigid wall stays where it was.

twin.prompt: A plant cell has become plasmolysed. What has happened to the size of its vacuole?
options: it has become smaller
it has become larger
it has stayed the same
twin.explain: Water has left the vacuole by osmosis, so it has shrunk, and so has the cytoplasm.

optionNotes.option: it has become larger
optionNotes.why: A larger vacuole is what a turgid cell has; a plasmolysed cell has lost water.

optionNotes.option: it has stayed the same
optionNotes.why: The water that left came out of the vacuole and cytoplasm, so they shrink.

alt: A plasmolysed cell put into pure water. Water moves in because the cell sap is now the more concentrated solution; the vacuole swells, the membrane presses back on the wall and the cell is turgid again.

caption: Put the plasmolysed cell in pure water and the direction reverses.

md: A plasmolysed cell put into **pure water** recovers. Now the cell sap is the **more concentrated** liquid, so water moves **in**: the vacuole and cytoplasm swell, the membrane presses back against the wall, and the cell becomes **turgid**.
A full answer has three parts: water moves **in**, **across the selectively permeable membrane**, **from the dilute solution to the more concentrated** one.

stem: Celery cells plasmolysed in strong salt solution are then put into pure water. Explain how osmosis changes the cells. [3]

steps.working: Water moves into the cells.
steps.decision: The pure water outside is the dilute liquid; the cell sap is the concentrated one.

steps.working: It crosses the selectively permeable cell membrane.
steps.decision: Naming the membrane's property is a mark of its own.

steps.working: It moves from the dilute water to the more concentrated sap, so the vacuole swells and the cells become turgid.
steps.decision: Direction, then result: the membrane returns to the wall.

prompt: Plasmolysed onion cells are put into pure water for an hour. Which describes them afterwards?
options: turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
plasmolysed, with the membrane still away from the wall
burst, with the cell wall split open
answer: turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
explain: The cell sap is now more concentrated than the pure water, so water moves in, the vacuole swells and the membrane presses back on the wall: turgid. The celery cells in the See it recovered the same way.

optionNotes.option: plasmolysed, with the membrane still away from the wall
optionNotes.why: That ignores the new surroundings: in pure water the sap is the stronger liquid, so water comes back in.

optionNotes.option: burst, with the cell wall split open
optionNotes.why: The cell wall limits the entry of water, so a plant cell becomes turgid rather than bursting.

twin.prompt: Turgid potato cells are put into a strong sucrose solution for an hour. Which describes them afterwards?
options: plasmolysed, with the membrane pulled away from the wall
turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
burst, with the membrane split
twin.answer: plasmolysed, with the membrane pulled away from the wall
twin.explain: The sucrose solution is more concentrated than the sap, so water leaves, the contents shrink and the membrane pulls away from the wall.

optionNotes.option: turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
optionNotes.why: They stay turgid only in a weaker solution; this one is stronger, so water leaves.

optionNotes.option: burst, with the membrane split
optionNotes.why: Cells burst only when too much water enters; here water is leaving.

text: 5. Why a plant cell does not burst

alt: Cells in pure water. A red blood cell swells and then bursts, because it has no cell wall. A plant cell becomes turgid and stops there, because its cell wall limits the entry of water.

A red blood cell swells and then bursts, because it has no cell wall. A plant cell becomes turgid and stops there, because its cell wall limits the entry of water.</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><ellipse cx="60" cy="80" rx="34" ry="22"/><path d="M100 80 L123 80" fill="none"/><path d="M132 80 L123 84.5 L123 75.5 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="166" cy="80" r="28"/><path d="M232 60 L240 72 L230 84 L244 98 M262 56 L256 70 L268 84 L258 100" fill="none"/><rect x="280" y="35" width="100" height="90" rx="10" fill="none" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="284" y="39" width="92" height="82" rx="10" fill="none"/><circle cx="296" cy="51" r="5" fill="currentColor"/></g><g fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.18" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"><ellipse cx="334" cy="80" rx="28.5" ry="25.4"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="60" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">red cell</text><text x="166" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">swells</text><text x="250" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">bursts</text><text x="330" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">plant cell:</text><text x="330" y="164" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="600">turgid</text><text x="10" y="200" font-size="14">both in pure water: the wall limits the entry of water</text></g></svg>
caption: Same water, two endings: the cell wall is the difference.

md: In pure water, a plant cell takes in water until it is turgid. The **cell wall** will then stretch no further, so it **limits the entry of water** and the cell does not burst.
An animal cell, such as a red blood cell, has **no cell wall**. Water keeps entering until the membrane bursts. In a concentrated solution the same animal cell loses water and shrinks.

stem: A spinach leaf cell and a red blood cell are each put into pure water. Describe and explain what happens to each. [4]

steps.working: Water moves into both cells by osmosis.
steps.decision: Pure water is more dilute than the contents of either cell.

steps.working: The red blood cell swells and bursts.
steps.decision: Nothing outside its membrane stops it stretching.

steps.working: The spinach cell becomes turgid but does not burst,
steps.decision: Name the result for the plant cell before the reason.

steps.working: because its cell wall limits the entry of water.
steps.decision: The wall is the one structure the red blood cell lacks.

prompt: A turgid plant cell in pure water takes in no more water. Which statement explains why?
options: its cell wall will not stretch any further, so it limits the entry of water
its cell membrane has stopped letting water through
its vacuole has stopped osmosis
answer: its cell wall will not stretch any further, so it limits the entry of water
explain: The rigid wall pushes back once the cell is full, so no more water can enter and the cell cannot burst. In the See it the spinach cell stopped at turgid for that reason.

optionNotes.option: its cell membrane has stopped letting water through
optionNotes.why: The membrane still lets water through; it is the wall that stops the cell swelling further.

optionNotes.option: its vacuole has stopped osmosis
optionNotes.why: The vacuole is where the water goes; it does not control the membrane or the wall.

twin.prompt: A red blood cell is put into pure water and bursts. Which statement explains why?
options: it has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
sugar from the water enters and splits it
its vacuole fills and splits
twin.answer: it has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
twin.explain: Water keeps entering by osmosis, and with no wall to push back the membrane stretches until it bursts.

optionNotes.option: sugar from the water enters and splits it
optionNotes.why: Pure water has no sugar in it; it is water entering by osmosis that swells the cell.

optionNotes.option: its vacuole fills and splits
optionNotes.why: A red blood cell has no large vacuole; the whole cell swells until its membrane bursts.

md: In Prescribed Practical B5 the cylinders rarely start at the same mass, so a raw change in grams cannot be compared fairly. A **percentage change** compares each change with its own starting mass.
**percentage change = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100**. Give the change its **+** or **−** sign, and round to one decimal place, keeping a trailing zero: 14.0, never 14.

stem: A potato cylinder of 2.50 g weighs 2.85 g when it comes out of water the next day. Find the percentage change, correct to 1 decimal place. [2]

steps.working: Change in mass = 2.85 − 2.50 = +0.35 g
steps.decision: Final minus start, so the sign shows a gain.
Divide by the mass at the start; write the trailing zero for one decimal place.

prompt: A 3.20 g potato cylinder weighs 2.88 g after a day in strong sugar solution. Give the percentage change, correct to 1 decimal place.
explain: Change = 2.88 − 3.20 = −0.32 g, and −0.32 ÷ 3.20 × 100 = −10.0 per cent. The divisor is the starting mass, as in the See it, and the minus sign shows a loss.

twin.prompt: A 4.80 g potato cylinder weighs 5.16 g after a day in water. Give the percentage change, correct to 1 decimal place.

caption: Gains plot above zero, losses below it. Where the line crosses zero, inside and outside match.

md: Plot the concentration of the solution along the bottom and the percentage change up the side, with the zero line part-way up, because some cylinders lose mass and plot **below** it.
Where the line crosses zero there is no change in mass, so the cell sap is **as concentrated as** that solution. That reading is how the practical finds the concentration of the cell sap.

stem: Use the graph to find the concentration of sucrose solution with the same concentration as the potato's cell sap, and explain your answer. [2]

steps.working: The line crosses zero at 6 per cent.
steps.decision: Read along the zero line, then down to the concentration axis.

steps.working: No change in mass there, so no net movement of water: the sap is as concentrated as 6 per cent sucrose.
steps.decision: Zero change means equal concentrations, not that osmosis has stopped.

prompt: On the graph of potato cylinders in sucrose solutions, what happens to a cylinder in 12 per cent sucrose?
options: it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
its mass does not change
answer: it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
explain: At 12 per cent the line is below zero, so the cylinder loses mass: the solution is stronger than the sap, water leaves, and the cells plasmolyse. The See it found the sap matches 6 per cent; anything stronger draws water out.

optionNotes.option: it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
optionNotes.why: Gains are above the zero line; at 12 per cent the line is well below it.

optionNotes.option: its mass does not change
optionNotes.why: No change is only where the line crosses zero, at 6 per cent.

twin.prompt: On the same graph, what happens to a cylinder in 2 per cent sucrose?
options: it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
its mass does not change
twin.answer: it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
twin.explain: At 2 per cent the line is above zero: the solution is weaker than the sap, so water enters and the cells become turgid.

optionNotes.option: it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
optionNotes.why: Losses are below the zero line; at 2 per cent the line is above it.

optionNotes.option: its mass does not change
optionNotes.why: No change is only at 6 per cent, where the line crosses zero.

md: **Visking tubing** is a model of the cell membrane: water passes through it, sucrose does not. Knot a length at one end, fill it with a solution, knot the other end, dry it and weigh it. Stand it in a second solution, then dry and reweigh it.
Compare the inside with the outside, exactly as for a cell. A bag that loses water ends **smaller and limp**; one that gains ends **swollen and firm**. Water moves, never the sucrose.

stem: Three bags stand in 5 per cent sucrose for 24 hours. Bag 1 (water inside) goes from 20.4 g to 18.8 g, bag 2 (5 per cent) stays at 20.9 g, bag 3 (20 per cent) goes from 21.6 g to 24.4 g. Explain the three results. [3]

steps.working: Bag 1: −1.6 g, −7.8 per cent. The outside is stronger, so water leaves the bag.
steps.decision: Water moves out through the tubing into the more concentrated solution.

steps.working: Bag 2: 0.0 g, 0.0 per cent. Inside and outside are equal, so there is no net movement.
steps.decision: Equal concentrations: the third case, as for the potato.

steps.working: Bag 3: +2.8 g, +13.0 per cent. The inside is stronger, so water enters.
steps.decision: The sucrose stays inside; only water crosses the tubing.

prompt: Four Visking bags hold the same sucrose solution and stand in 0, 5, 10 and 15 per cent sucrose. Their percentage changes in mass are +31, +12, −6 and −15. What could the concentration inside the bags be?
options: between 5 and 10 per cent
between 0 and 5 per cent
between 10 and 15 per cent
explain: The bags gain mass up to 5 per cent and lose it from 10 per cent, so the change crosses zero between them: the inside matches a concentration between 5 and 10 per cent. In the See it, the bag that matched its outside did not change.

optionNotes.option: between 0 and 5 per cent
optionNotes.why: Bags still gained mass at 5 per cent, so the inside was stronger than 5 per cent.

optionNotes.option: between 10 and 15 per cent
optionNotes.why: Bags already lost mass at 10 per cent, so the inside was weaker than 10 per cent.

twin.prompt: In the same set of four bags, why did the bag in 10 per cent sucrose lose mass?
options: water moved out of it into the more concentrated 10 per cent solution
sucrose moved out of it into the beaker
water moved into it from the 10 per cent solution
twin.answer: water moved out of it into the more concentrated 10 per cent solution
twin.explain: The 10 per cent outside was stronger than the inside, so water left the bag through the selectively permeable tubing.

optionNotes.option: sucrose moved out of it into the beaker
optionNotes.why: Sucrose molecules are too large to cross the tubing; only water moves.

optionNotes.option: water moved into it from the 10 per cent solution
optionNotes.why: Water moving in would make the bag gain mass; it lost mass.

md: **Every change signed** (2025). Booklet A gives a mark for a + or − in front of each change in mass.
**One decimal place, trailing zero kept** (2025). A percentage of 13 where 13.0 was asked loses the mark.
**Variables by name** (2025). Concentration of sucrose is independent; final mass is dependent; the volume of solution and the time are controlled.
**Two tissues compared** (2025). The tissue whose line crosses zero at the higher concentration has the more concentrated cell sap.

stem: Use the graph to say which tissue, radish or celery, has the more concentrated cell sap. [2]

steps.working: Radish crosses zero at 7 per cent; celery at 3 per cent.
steps.decision: Read each line where it meets the zero line.

steps.working: So radish cell sap is the more concentrated.
steps.decision: A higher crossing means a stronger solution was needed to stop the gain.

prompt: Carrot cylinders show no change in mass in 0.25 mol dm⁻³ sucrose and parsnip cylinders in 0.40 mol dm⁻³. Which has the more concentrated cell sap?
options: parsnip
carrot
they are the same
explain: No change in mass means the sap matches that solution, and parsnip matches the stronger one, 0.40 mol dm⁻³. In the See it, radish crossed zero later than celery for the same reason.

optionNotes.option: carrot
optionNotes.why: Carrot matches the weaker solution, 0.25 mol dm⁻³, so its sap is the more dilute.

optionNotes.option: they are the same
optionNotes.why: They stop changing at different concentrations, so their saps differ.

twin.prompt: Onion tissue shows no change in mass in 4 per cent sucrose and beetroot tissue in 9 per cent. Which has the more dilute cell sap?
options: onion
beetroot
they are the same
twin.explain: Onion's sap matches 4 per cent sucrose, the weaker solution, so its sap is the more dilute.

optionNotes.option: beetroot
optionNotes.why: Beetroot matches the stronger solution, 9 per cent, so its sap is the more concentrated.

optionNotes.option: they are the same
optionNotes.why: Different no-change concentrations mean different saps.

md: Osmosis comes on the B2 paper as a whole question of six to eight marks, and in Unit 7 as Prescribed Practical B5. Name both liquids and say which is stronger, give the direction of the water, name the selectively permeable membrane, then finish on what was asked: the level, the mass or the cells.
